name: Getting to Know the World's Greatest Composers: Ludwig van Beethoven (single complete volume by Mike Venezia)

routing.ruling: Curriculum, the closest call of the three same-evening Venezia drops, decided on the skills' own rules with Aless's one-word 'Curriculum' message weighed as a founder signal rather than an automatic override. Against curriculum: unlike the sibling drops this is a SINGLE 32-page trade biography, and a lone bound book with no scope-and-sequence resembles the toddler-activity-book precedent that went reference. For curriculum, and decisive: (1) this drop is the third file of one coherent same-hour wave of the same series family, and the curriculum skill's multi-book-wave rule analyzes a coherent set per drop rather than fragmenting the wave across two different skills with two different output shapes; (2) what Homa needs from this book is Layer-1/Layer-2 material (the composer-study methodology and its fit to the Music > Composer Study & Music Appreciation domain added earlier this session), not a per-page layout/print-format analysis of a book nobody will print; (3) the book itself carries real embedded listening pedagogy (what to listen for, movement by movement), which is method content, not printable-reference content. Aless's 'Curriculum' note agrees with this ruling, and it was treated as evidence about intended product use (a composer-study spine), not as the reason. If a future single-volume Venezia drop arrives outside a wave, reference routing with a method note would also be defensible; this one is curriculum.

layer1_philosophy.methodology: Biography-driven music appreciation: 'Getting to Know the World's Greatest Composers: Ludwig van Beethoven', written and illustrated by Mike Venezia, Children's Press (A Division of Grolier Publishing, New York/London/Hong Kong/Sydney, Danbury Connecticut), with a credited subject-expert consultant: Donald Freund, Professor of Composition, Indiana University School of Music. Identity verified directly from the cover and title page renders. Same core Venezia recipe as the artists volumes (humor plus real images plus simple prose, 32 standalone pages, no activities), adapted to music: since the subject's works cannot be printed on a page, the reproductions here are portraits, period paintings and prints, photographs, and sheet-music motifs on the endpapers, and the book compensates with explicit listening guidance woven through the prose, telling the child what to listen for in specific named works.
principles: The same humor-first on-ramp: the cover gag has an orchestra player picking up Beethoven's ear trumpet by mistake; interior panels imagine neighbors complaining about the racket and fans mobbing Ludwig in Vienna ('as popular as any rock star today')

Music is described by its feeling and its craft, not just named: Beethoven's best-known pieces are contrasted with the light, cheerful court music people expected ('loud and exciting, and often beautiful enough to give you goose bumps'), and the book teaches real structural vocabulary in context: a symphony 'usually has four parts, or movements', bigger orchestras, moods, and a theme that can be changed, disguised, or played in part to keep the audience guessing

Specific works get specific listening guidance: the Fifth Symphony's famous theme is 'only four notes long... you can hear them in the beginning', and the Sixth (Pastoral) is walked through as a story in sound: arriving in the countryside, a brook, villagers, a thunderstorm, a shepherd's thankful song, with the aside that Beethoven copied actual bird songs from nightingales, quails, and cuckoos

The life explains the work, told plainly including the hard parts: a harsh father who overworked a four-year-old at the keyboard, his mother's death, supporting his brothers, and deafness treated at length: hiding it, the letter to his brothers, composing while unable to hear, the Ninth's choral finale written when fully deaf

Historical context frames the person: the Age of Enlightenment, respect for everyday people over kings, Napoleon and the Eroica, Vienna as Europe's musical capital, Mozart and Haydn as the connecting cast

The book bridges to real listening rather than to museums: the closing page tells families Beethoven's music is easy to find on the radio and at the library on CD or cassette, and that a recording of the Fifth Symphony flew on Voyager 2 'as a sample of what human beings are all about'
layer1_philosophy.learningTheory: Same exposure-and-affection model as the sibling drops: love one composer as a person through story, then meet the actual music with a few concrete things to listen for. No protocol, no prerequisites; the volume is standalone within an unordered series. The embedded what-to-listen-for guidance makes this the most directly teachable volume of the three drops: it hands the parent a ready-made active-listening script for at least three named works.
layer1_philosophy.assessmentApproach: None: no questions, activities, or quizzes anywhere in the volume. Any narration or listening-response work comes from the family's own method.
layer1_philosophy.parentRole: Reader-aloud and listening companion: the text is written to the child at a grade 2-3 level, and the closing page explicitly sends the family to find recordings, making the parent the supplier of the actual music the book can only describe.

knowledgeBankGaps.title: Getting to Know the World's Greatest Composers Format (Mike Venezia)
knowledgeBankGaps.summary: 32-page standalone picture-book composer biographies, one composer per volume, written and illustrated by Mike Venezia (Children's Press / Grolier) with a credited composition-professor consultant. Same humor-plus-real-images recipe as the artists series, adapted to music: portraits and period art instead of artwork reproductions, sheet-music endpapers, and explicit in-prose listening guidance for named works (the Fifth's four-note theme, the Pastoral's five-scene story, the Ninth's choral finale). Closes by sending families to real recordings (radio, library, Voyager 2 aside) rather than museums. This drop: the Ludwig van Beethoven volume, complete.
